title_de: #1 Passer-Rating? Purdys historische Statistiken im Check
title_en: No. 1 in passer rating? Purdy’s historic numbers checked
teaser_de: Steht Brock Purdy mit einem Karriere-Passer-Rating von 105,6 zu Recht an der Spitze der ewigen Bestenliste? Gegenproben mit ANY/A und Total QBR und ein Blick auf die noch kleine Stichprobe.
teaser_en: Does Brock Purdy belong at the top of the all-time list with a career passer rating of 105.6? Cross-checks with ANY/A and Total QBR and a look at the still small sample.
body_en:
## No. 1 in NFL history: Brock Purdy takes the passer rating throne

Since passing the 1,500-attempt mark, Purdy has led the all-time list in passer rating at 105.6. This article puts into context how solid this record is after 54 regular-season games, what the metric ignores, and what ANY/A and ESPN's Total QBR show as cross-checks.

## 1,500 pass attempts and first place

For its career leaderboards, Pro Football Reference requires at least 1,500 pass attempts, a mark Purdy reached after six games of the 2026 season with 1,524 passes and 86 sacks, i.e. 1,610 dropbacks. Since then, the last pick of the 2022 draft has topped the all-time list with a passer rating of 105.6, ahead of Lamar Jackson (102.7), Aaron Rodgers (101.8), Joe Burrow (101.3) and Patrick Mahomes (100.8). That is remarkable for a quarterback with just three and a half years as a starter, but it also raises questions: how solid is a record after comparatively few games, and what does passer rating actually measure?

The answer is more complex than it seems at first glance, which is why it is worth looking at three metrics that view the same phenomenon from different angles. Passer rating and ANY/A both work exclusively with box-score ingredients, while ESPN's Total QBR evaluates every action in context. The data comes from Pro Football Reference and ESPN; the analysis is my own calculation.

## Passer rating: what the number can and can't do

The classic passer rating is fed by four box-score figures: completion percentage, yards per attempt, touchdown rate and interception rate. Precisely because of that, it has two structural weaknesses worth keeping in mind with a record value: it ignores sacks completely, so a quarterback who holds the ball too long isn't penalized for it, and it has no game context, neither down and distance nor score or opponent. Leading the ANY/A list is therefore only of limited use as additional evidence, since both metrics are made from the same ingredients, and whoever leads in one formula will almost inevitably rank near the top in the other. Real cross-checks only come from metrics that include sacks and account for context, and that is what the following sections are about.

## ANY/A: efficiency per dropback

The formula Pro Football Reference uses for its career list is: (passing yards − sack yards + 20 × touchdowns − 45 × interceptions) / (pass attempts + sacks). At its core, ANY/A builds on simple yards per attempt but corrects it in three places that are crucial for evaluating a quarterback:

- **Sacks** are treated like a pass attempt with negative yardage, so a quarterback who holds the ball too long is noticeably penalized.
- **Touchdowns** earn a 20-yard bonus, because a pass into the end zone is worth more than the yards it covers.
- **Interceptions** cost a flat 45 yards, which is meant to roughly reflect the value of a turnover including the change in field position.

Since all of these stats have been recorded for more than 60 years, this stat at least allows a historical comparison of all QBs who have played in the NFL since the '50s. At 8.00, Purdy tops the all-time list here as well, with a lead of 0.61 over Patrick Mahomes, almost as large as the entire gap between Mahomes in second place and Russell Wilson in 16th.

| Rank | Quarterback | Career ANY/A |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brock Purdy | 8.00 |
| 2 | Patrick Mahomes | 7.39 |
| 3 | Lamar Jackson | 7.32 |
| 4 | Peyton Manning | 7.17 |
| 5 | Aaron Rodgers | 7.14 |

Source: Pro Football Reference, as of October 20, 2026.

But does that really make Purdy the most efficient quarterback in NFL history? The most obvious objection concerns the era, since the league average in ANY/A has risen from 4.9 in 1985 to 6.1 in the current season, mainly due to fewer interceptions, fewer sacks and rules that have systematically protected the passing game. If you strip out this era effect and compare each quarterback with the dropback-weighted league average of his own seasons, Purdy still leads at +2.00 yards above average, followed by Steve Young (+1.68), Peyton Manning (+1.61), Joe Montana (+1.55) and Dan Marino (+1.42), while Mahomes only comes in sixth at +1.29. So the modern era alone does not explain Purdy's position.

## QBR: context counts

Passer rating and ANY/A treat an 8-yard pass on 3rd and 12 exactly like one on 3rd and 6; they don't distinguish between garbage time and the two-minute drill and ignore what the quarterback does with his legs. This is exactly where Total QBR comes in, which ESPN has published since 2011 and which differs from ANY/A in three key respects:

- **Situation instead of box score.** Every action gets a value based on expected points from down, distance and field position. According to ESPN, a third-down conversion is worth about +2.1 points, while an interception costs about 4.2 points.
- **All of the quarterback's actions.** Besides passes and sacks, designed runs, scrambles and turnovers are included as well, while a simple handoff earns the quarterback nothing.
- **Opponent and score.** There is more credit against strong defenses and less against weak ones, and anyone playing with a big lead or deficit gets less credit for the same action. For passes, the model also splits the value between pass protection, the throw, the catch and yards after the catch.

The result is converted to a scale from 0 to 100, with 50 corresponding to the league average. Because QBR is a value per action, it measures efficiency, like ANY/A, not volume.

| QBR | Classification over a season |
|---|---|
| 25 | Replacement level |
| 50 | League average |
| 65 to 70 | Pro Bowl level (according to ESPN, 2011) |
| 75 and up | Elite |

If you combine the season values since 2006 into a dropback-weighted career QBR, a more nuanced picture than with passer rating emerges among the 76 quarterbacks with more than 1,500 passes: Purdy ranks third at 71.4, behind Peyton Manning and Patrick Mahomes.

| Rank | Quarterback | Career QBR | Passes since 2006 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Peyton Manning | 75.5 | 5,047 |
| 2 | Patrick Mahomes | 72.2 | 4,831 |
| 3 | Brock Purdy | 71.4 | 1,524 |
| 4 | Drew Brees | 70.5 | 8,742 |
| 5 | Tom Brady | 70.5 | 9,502 |

Source: ESPN Total QBR via Pro Football Reference, seasons 2006–2026, as of October 20, 2026, my own calculation (average of season values, weighted by dropbacks).

Note that Manning's value only covers his years from 2006 to 2015, because ESPN's QBR only starts in 2006, and that Purdy's value is based on just 1,524 passes, while Brees and Brady each contributed more than 8,700 passes to the average. His strong start to the 2026 season at 85.8 also lifts his average, but more on that later.

Another catch deserves mention, though: ESPN does not publish an official career value, which is why the average of the season values is used here, weighted by dropbacks. In addition, ESPN changed the model several times between 2011 and 2016, among other things by valuing interceptions based on the expected return, including pressure and introducing a new points model, which is why comparisons across many years are a good guide but not an exact yardstick.

## Where the two metrics diverge

Things get interesting where ANY/A and QBR reach different verdicts. The lists are not exactly comparable, since ANY/A covers the entire career while QBR only starts in 2006. Josh Allen is only 17th on the all-time ANY/A list at 6.72, because his rushing touchdowns don't generate 20-yard bonuses in the passing game, while in career QBR he ranks sixth at 67.2, since runs and scrambles count there. With Lamar Jackson, despite his rushing skills, it is the other way around: he is third in ANY/A but only eighth in QBR (66.7), and Patrick Mahomes ranks second on both lists. The fact that Purdy ranks first in ANY/A and third in QBR, even though one metric disadvantages scramblers and the other accounts for them, is probably the strongest indication that his result is not a quirk of a single formula.

## The comparison with Garoppolo and Tua

The most revealing comparison is with Jimmy Garoppolo, because both compiled their numbers largely in the same scheme, under the same head coach and partly with the same weapons. So one might ask whether Purdy's numbers simply reflect the Shanahan system. A second point of comparison is Tua Tagovailoa, who from 2022 on played in a related offense in Miami under Mike McDaniel, a Shanahan disciple. The cross-check is clear:

| Metric | Purdy | Garoppolo | Tagovailoa |
|---|---|---|---|
| Career ANY/A | 8.00 | 6.97 | 6.60 |
| Career QBR (since 2006) | 71.4 | 57.1 | 55.5 |
| Rank on the QBR list (76 quarterbacks) | 3 | 29 | 35 |
| Passes since 2006 | 1,524 | 1,936 | 2,421 |

Source: Pro Football Reference, ESPN Total QBR, as of October 20, 2026, my own calculation. The QBR values include all seasons since 2006 with a QBR value, so for Garoppolo also the weak 2023 Raiders year.

The neighbors on the list are interesting too, because between Purdy and the two comparison players there are around 14 and 16 QBR points respectively, and a whole series of names. Purdy sits between Patrick Mahomes (72.2) and Drew Brees (70.5), Garoppolo at 29th between Kirk Cousins (57.8) and C.J. Stroud (56.2), Tagovailoa at 35th between Carson Wentz (55.6) and Eli Manning (55.4). With Tagovailoa, there is also the fact that his QBR fell from 70.6 in 2022 to 61.5, 57.1 and most recently 37.5, while Purdy's season values range between 64.8 and 85.8.

With Garoppolo, the comparison can be taken further with other metrics: in adjusted EPA per play, Purdy is clearly ahead of Garoppolo at 0.279 to 0.173, in success rate at 53.9% to 50.0% and in CPOE at +4.0 to +0.4. It is remarkable that Garoppolo's nominal completion rate of 68.4% is actually higher than Purdy's 66.5%. So at an average of 7.3 air yards per pass (Purdy: 8.0), Garoppolo completed the easier passes and Purdy the harder ones, and Purdy still keeps the offense on schedule more often. The system raises the floor a quarterback stands on, but how high he jumps from there still depends on anticipation, accuracy and decision-making.

## The honest counter-calculation

However, it would be too simple to just celebrate the numbers, because several caveats belong to the overall picture. First, the sample is comparatively small: Purdy's 8.00 is based on 1,610 dropbacks, while Manning or Brady each accumulated more than 10,000, including all their injury and aging years. In addition, the record value so far rests mainly on two outliers, the 2023 season at 9.01 and the current year at 9.21 from only 176 dropbacks so far. Without the 2026 start, his career value would be 7.85, and without 2023 as well, about 7.28, which would still be above Peyton Manning's career value of 7.17. So Purdy has not yet played a below-average season in his career; he has simply had two exceptional ones.

QBR, too, has to be read with caution, since the career QBR of 71.4 includes the strong 85.8 from the 2026 start, while his 2022 rookie year at 67.5 pulls the average down a bit again. On top of that, both metrics only reflect the regular season: Purdy's ANY/A in the playoffs is 6.9 from eight games and therefore noticeably below his career value. But here, too, every season was well above the league average of just under 57.

And finally, total value over a career paints a different picture than efficiency per dropback. If you multiply the margin over the league average by the number of dropbacks, Manning and Brady each produced around 15,500 yards above average for their teams, Purdy so far a little over 3,200. He will therefore have to earn his place in history over time.

## Conclusion

So what remains of the passer rating record? Passer rating and ANY/A are related box-score formulas, QBR evaluates every action in context, and the fact that Brock Purdy is at the very top in all three metrics is probably less a coincidence than a pattern, even if Peyton Manning and Patrick Mahomes are still ahead of him in career QBR. What is exceptional is less the individual record value than the consistency behind it, since in every one of his seasons so far he has been at least one yard above the league average in ANY/A, and that under a head coach with whom quarterbacks such as Nick Mullens, C.J. Beathard or Trey Lance did not produce comparable numbers over a longer period. At the same time, after 54 regular-season games it remains more of an interim result than a legacy, and the real test is still to come: holding this level even when Kittle, McCaffrey and co. are past their peak because of age.

If you want to read more and take a closer look at the numbers, feel free to continue on my stats pages.

[QBR career stats: leaderboard and chart](https://cp7.beer/projects/qbr-career-stats/)

I hope this overview helps you bring a few more arguments to the next Purdy discussion with friends or in the comment sections.

**Go Niners!**
